doc.title: Robert Glasper interviewed by Greg Thomas, Clinton, New York, February 20, 2016

title: Church music, leaving his Harlem church, and touring musicians
summary: Answering Doc Woods, Glasper recounts playing in a Harlem church after arriving in New York and leaving when touring made it impossible.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: All right. I see a lot of heads shaking out there. So why don’t you all get up in this, all right? So if you’ve got a question or a comment raise your hand and partake. All right. This is Professor Michael “Doc” Woods, Professor of Music here for many years.
Hello, sir. Nice to meet you.

I’ll bet you’re a musician. MW: Your church background I think is just fabulous. Do you see any way in the immediate future on your event horizon where you can kind of revolutionize, particularly in black churches, what the black pastors will let the young musicians do?

I think that’s already changing. Granted, they kicked me out of church in ’99. Footnote, I got kicked out. But thank God, when I was playing in church in Houston when I got a scholarship to come to New York, my pastor in Houston led this church called Brentwood Baptist Church, and my pastor said, “I’m going to call my boy up in Harlem and you’re going to play at his church when you get there.” So I had a good job the first week I got to New York. I got to New York, they put me over to the male chorus first of all, I’m 17 or 18 years old over the male chorus, I’m like, “no!” They were horrible, it was really bad. And then a few months after that they put me on the teen choir so it was like yes. So the teen choir was cool. At that point I started getting calls from, like I said, Christian McBride and I started going out of town. And at that point it wasn’t cool to go out of town. I mean you’ve got to be at church. So after a while it was like I had to make a decision, to be here or not. So I said I had to leave. It’s now become cool for your music director to be gone, because the pastor can say, “our music director is out with Mary J. Blige this Sunday.” You know. And when you get back from tour, all my friends that still play in church tell me that, I’ve got a bunch of cats that play with everybody and the pastor comes back and, “so our bassist just got back from the road from the Beyoncé tour.” So it makes it hard — it gives the church a little popping thing. Who did your piano player play for? You know. So I think now it’s become a lot more acceptable. You know what I mean? And you know I think that’s just the culture now. You know? You do other stuff and I play at this church. It’s almost like giving the church publicity when you’re on the road a lot of times. Because the people want to kind of — the people want to go to the church that has the really good music as well. The younger people tend to want to go to the church with good music. Older people want to go to church for the good preacher. So if you have both it’s great. The best choir, the best musicians get a lot of the younger people. You know what I mean?
